lines.text: This is OceanScope. The North Indian Ocean, rebuilt in three dimensions, from the waves at the surface to four thousand metres below.
In July, the southwest monsoon drives a heavy swell across the Arabian Sea.
Off Somalia, the Great Whirl spins up: an eddy five hundred kilometres wide.
Along the Lakshadweep and Maldives ridge, coral shoals glow in shallow water.
lines.say: Along the Luck-shud-weep and Maldives ridge, coral shoals glow in shallow water.

lines.text: In the Bay of Bengal, river water floats on top as a warm, fresh lid.
And in May 2020, that warm water fed Cyclone Amphan, one of the strongest storms the Bay has ever seen.
lines.say: And in May twenty twenty, that warm water fed Cyclone Um-pun, one of the strongest storms the Bay has ever seen.

lines.text: OceanScope lets you cut the ocean open like a cake. Slice along any line, switch between temperature, salinity and currents, and peel back the layers.
Every wave is live. Push the sea state to a storm, or paint the surface with real data.
Click anywhere on the water to dive in. You get the whole water column: temperature, salt, sound speed, cyclone fuel, model error, and who lives at every depth.
The Truth Meter shows where the ocean model disagrees with real Argo floats, and ranks the places that most need a new float.
Cyclone Lab replays Amphan day by day. The fuel gauge rises, the storm intensifies, and a cold wake spreads behind it.
lines.say: Cyclone Lab replays Um-pun day by day. The fuel gauge rises, the storm intensifies, and a cold wake spreads behind it.

lines.text: For search and rescue, drop the last known position. Seven hundred virtual drifters ride the currents and rank where to search first.
Sonar traces sound through the water and finds the quiet zones where a submarine can hide.
Learn mode turns it all into a story, with marine life at every depth, quizzes, and the Arabian Sea's low oxygen zone.
And a built-in copilot drives everything in plain English.
Ask where to deploy the next float, and it answers from the model's own blind spots.
From the sunlit surface to the midnight zone, every layer tells a story.
OceanScope. See the ocean the way scientists do.
